Without updating weights, SYLVA reaches 82.1% completion in 64-agent simulations and 98.3% on live LLM workflows (vs. 0.0% single frozen LLM and 45.6% static MCP/A2A), cuts false specialist penalties by 6.79x-10.8x, retains 86.2% creator revenue under wrapper/Sybil floods, and recovers rapidly after rule drift. Furthermore, 1-call skill compilation saves 78.3% of real LLM tokens, while our Starknet contracts verify zero-oracle quorum slashing and 32.32-bit fixed-point (Q32.32) routing on-chain. Code and contracts are at https://github.com/heurion-org/sylva.

item.title: Twice-Told Critiques: Claim-Level Homogenization of Peer Review in the LLM Era
item.description: Peer review relies on several readers finding different problems. We measure critique overlap in conference and journal reviews. At ICLR, measured overlap rose from 12.0% in 2026 to 21.3% in 2027, in reviews from the same stage of the review process, with year-on-year rises at NeurIPS, ICML and the F1000 and PLOS journals. A third ICLR review of a paper added 5.46 new problems to the other two in 2027, against 6.12 in 2026. We apply MELD, a detector of LLM-generated text, to all reviews. Within a paper, two reviews that MELD flags overlap more than two unflagged reviews: by 3.0 points at ICLR in 2024-2025, by 4.5 points in 2026-2027, and by 5.4 points across five journal sources. These results provide evidence that LLM-flagged reviews of one paper are less distinct from each other than unflagged reviews, and suggest that the diversity of critiques among reviews of a single paper is falling.

item.title: What If Chain-of-Thought Is Not Enough?
item.description: Reasoning capabilities in large language models have evolved from prompting-based methods to internalized model behaviors. In this paper, we investigate whether the internal thinking model of an LLM can be deliberately changed and whether such a change is beneficial. Instead of relying on Chain-of-Thought, we train models to follow Question--Option--Criteria (QOC), a structured decision process that decomposes a task into explicit questions, competing options, and evaluation criteria. We present a three-generation development pipeline that ranges from a basic QOC decision core to richer answer synthesis and statistically enriched QOC reasoning. We then evaluate the resulting models with respect to both internal consistency and output quality. Across the reported experiments, QOC-based fine-tuning improves answer quality relative to non-fine-tuned base models and yields particularly strong gains once models are large enough to execute the underlying QOC computations reliably. The results suggest that the internal thinking model of an LLM is trainable and that structured alternatives to Chain-of-Thought can provide a promising path toward more reliable, interpretable, and task-adapted decision support.

item.title: An asymptotic bound for Yuster's independent transversal factor conjecture
item.description: An $[r,n,1]$-graph has $r$ independent parts of size $n$, with a matching between each pair of parts. Yuster conjectured in 2021 that every such graph has a partition into independent transversals whenever $n\ge 2\lceil r/2\rceil$. We prove that there is an absolute constant $A>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $r$, this partition exists whenever $n\ge\lceil r+A r^{20/21}\rceil$. Thus $f(r)\le r+O(r^{20/21})$, where $f(r)$ is the least $n_0$ such that every $[r,n,1]$-graph has such a partition whenever $n\ge n_0$. In particular, $f(r)/r\to1$, giving an asymptotic form of the conjecture.

item.title: Invariance and Expressiveness: Modal Variations
item.description: This contribution focuses on bisimulation invariance as the hallmark of modal model theory and of modal modelling. It exemplifies traditional as well as more recent ramifications \&\ extensions of classical results -- involving variant modes of bisimulation equivalence and matching modalities also beyond plain Kripke structures, and emphasising especially the technical challenges in finite model theory and other non-elementary settings. Main results to be discussed revolve about the theme of expressive completeness phenomena: beside expressive completeness under bisimulation invariance in relation to first-order background logics, in the style of van Benthem--Rosen characterisations, this also concerns maximality results under criteria form abstract model theory, in the style of Lindstroem theorems.

item.title: Sharp topological overlap in every dimension
item.description: For a positive integer $d$ let $c_d^{\mathrm{top}}$ (resp. $c_d^{\mathrm{aff}}$) be the maximum $c$ such that, for every continuous (resp. affine) map from the $n$-dimensional simplex $Δ^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^d$, some point of $\mathbb{R}^d$ lies in the images of at least $(c-o(1))\binom{n+1}{d+1}$ of the $d$-dimensional faces, as $n\to\infty$. We show that \[ c_d^{\mathrm{top}}=c_d^{\mathrm{aff}}=\frac{(d+1)!}{(d+1)^{d+1}}. \] The second equality confirms a conjecture of Bukh, Matoušek, and Nivasch, who established the upper bound. The proof was found by GPT-6 Astra, following the directions of the author.

item.title: The Necessity of Acceptance & Rejection in Inferential Reasoning
item.description: In this paper, we argue that acceptance and rejection constitute two fundamental positions necessary for inferential reasoning. Our central thesis is that a proposition acquires an inferential role when it is considered from a position of acceptance or rejection, rather than purely understood as propositional content. We distinguish between understanding a proposition, entertaining it hypothetically, and employing it within an inference. Particular attention is given to hypothetical reasoning and suspended judgement, which appear to challenge the necessity of adopting either position. We maintain that these cases do not undermine our thesis, since inferential reasoning can involve provisional acceptance or rejection without requiring personal belief or permanent commitment. Accordingly, the necessity of these positions should be understood as inferential rather than psychological. By examining the relationship between propositional content, inferential positions, and rational commitment, we defend the view that acceptance and rejection provide the fundamental conditions under which propositions can function within reasoning. This establishes a philosophical foundation for understanding inference through opposed rational positions.

item.title: Learn, Freeze, and Transfer an Activation Function Across Architectures
item.description: Transfer learning typically reuses knowledge acquired by a source network through its learned weights. We investigate whether a learned activation function can also be transferred and remain useful in networks trained from scratch. We study this complementary form of transfer through a learn-freeze-transfer protocol, in which the activation is optimized jointly with a source network in a single training run, and is then frozen and reused in target networks trained from scratch. A pointwise activation with globally shared parameters is independent of layer dimensions and can therefore be incorporated into networks of different architectures trained from scratch. We instantiate this protocol with FAct, a five-parameter activation represented by a two-harmonic truncated Fourier series, initialized from a Fourier approximation of GELU and learned in a Vision Transformer (ViT) on ImageNet-1K. When reused in a ViT of the same architecture trained from scratch on ImageNet-1K, the frozen activation (Frozen FAct) improves top-1 accuracy by 1.46 percentage points over GELU. Across four smaller target architectures (standard ViT, Swin Transformer, linear-attention ViT, and MLP-Mixer) and four image-classification datasets, it achieves the highest mean accuracy among eleven activation functions in 15 of 16 settings under a common training configuration, with improvements of up to 1.71 percentage points over the best conventional activation. When the learning rate and weight decay are tuned separately for each activation under the same search budget, Frozen FAct still ranks first in 11 of the 16 settings, second in four, and fourth in one. These results provide empirical evidence that a learned activation function can retain its usefulness when transferred across vision architectures, independently of the weights with which it was learned.

item.title: Backbone Matters: Benchmarking Encoder-Decoder Networks for Semantic Segmentation of Driving Scenes on BDD100K
item.description: Semantic segmentation gives an autonomous vehicle a dense, pixel-level description of its surroundings and is a core part of scene understanding. Most segmentation networks consist of an encoder (the backbone) and a decoder, yet the backbone is often chosen without a systematic comparison. This work studies this choice on the BDD100K driving dataset. Four widely used decoders (U-Net, FPN, LinkNet and PSPNet) are combined with 13 backbones from six families (ResNet, VGG, DenseNet, Inception, MobileNet and EfficientNet), and all 52 models are trained with one common protocol. The best model, an FPN decoder with an EfficientNet-B4 backbone, reaches 62.6% mean intersection over union (mIoU), 89.8% accuracy and a loss of 0.092. Only two of the 52 models, both FPN with EfficientNet, exceed the 56.9% mIoU reported with the BDD100K benchmark. The effect of the backbone depends strongly on the decoder: the same EfficientNet-B4 gives 42.6% mIoU with PSPNet but 62.6% with FPN, and the gap between the best and the worst backbone ranges from 12.0 points (U-Net) to 42.5 points (FPN). The results and the scope of this study are discussed.

item.title: Cohomological $k$-Equivalence Does Not Capture Graph Isomorphism
item.description: Ó Conghaile introduced cohomological $k$-equivalence $\equiv^{\mathbb{Z}}_k$, a refinement of equivalence in $k$-variable counting logic that is decidable in polynomial time for each fixed $k$: the local isomorphisms that survive must extend, in both directions, to compatible families of integer combinations of local isomorphisms. He asked whether, for every finite relational signature $σ$, some $k$ makes $\equiv^{\mathbb{Z}}_k$ coincide with isomorphism of $σ$-structures (Question 14 of his MFCS 2022 paper). We show that the answer is negative already for graphs: for every $k\ge 1$ there are finite simple graphs $A_k\not\cong B_k$ with $A_k\equiv^{\mathbb{Z}}_k B_k$. Every isomorphism of the pair would induce a permutation $g$ of a common index set $D$. One part of the graphs, over $\mathbb{F}_3$, admits exactly the even permutations, because $g$ acts by its sign on a nonzero class in the cokernel of the unsigned boundary map on subsets of $D$. A second part, over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and built on the Johnson graph $J(|D|,2)$, admits exactly the odd permutations. No set of at most $k$ vertices detects the parity: every local isomorphism of a common family is realised, with the same images, by permutations of both parities. We complement the main result with three observations. For the pair built from an index set of size $n$, the least width at which cohomological equivalence distinguishes the two graphs is $\log_4 n+O(1)$; so within this construction the doubly exponential size is unavoidable. The pairs are nevertheless distinguished in polynomial time by an explicit invariant that combines the class of the part over $\mathbb{F}_3$ with the parity of the part over $\mathbb{F}_2$. Finally, cohomological $2$-equivalence already distinguishes the coloured graphs with which Berkholz and Grohe show that no level of the Diophantine relaxation decides isomorphism.

item.title: NariQ: Sub-3-Bit Quantization for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks
item.description: Long-horizon agentic tasks require a model to call tools over many steps at contexts of 100K tokens or more, yet many low-bit quantization methods are calibrated on short web text and judged on perplexity. This mismatch is costly: existing quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B at or below 3 bits per weight match BF16 on shorter tasks like AIME, yet in published results solve at most 72% as many tasks as BF16 on DeepSWE, a long-horizon agentic benchmark. We propose NariQ, a trellis-coded post-training quantization method that calibrates on tokens generated by the BF16 model in agent sessions. On Qwen3.8-27B, NariQ at 3.0 and 2.5 bits per weight stays level with BF16 on two long-horizon agentic benchmarks, DeepSWE and Terminal Bench, as well as on AIME and RealWorldQA. Our checkpoint at 2.0 bits per weight trails this performance. To our knowledge, these are the first quantizations at or below 3 bits per weight shown to match their full-precision version on long-horizon agentic tasks. We release the files as Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF (https://huggingface.co/nari-labs/Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF), with inference available through our llama.cpp fork at https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp.

item.title: Running-Time Lower Bounds under FPT $\neq$ W[1]
item.description: We revisit running-time lower bounds historically based on the Exponential Time Hypothesis. Our case study asks how much of their quantitative content can be recovered under the assumption FPT $\neq$ W[1]. The reductions encode the choice of a clique in few bits and control the target parameter in terms of that encoding. This makes a sufficiently fast algorithm for the target problem yield a fixed-parameter algorithm for deciding whether a graph has a clique of the requested size. We obtain twelve lower bounds for deterministic algorithms across graph, string, and integer feasibility problems, including bounds that hold under structural restrictions. In several cases the same function of the parameter appears in the exponent as in the historical bound, with the additional requirement that the cutoff for any prescribed saving in the exponent be computable.

item.title: Guided Cuckoo Filter: Full-Pipeline Insertion Optimization
item.description: Cuckoo filters are widely deployed as space-efficient alternatives to Bloom filters, supporting fast lookups, insertions, and deletions. However, their insertion cost grows steeply at high load factors because the standard insertion procedure is entirely unguided: it places each fingerprint into whichever candidate bucket happens to be tried first, and when both candidates are full, it displaces a random victim in a random walk. These blind random choices occur at two distinct stages of the insertion pipeline, the initial placement decision and the eviction victim selection, yet each stage can be independently replaced with a guided, informed decision. We propose the \emph{Guided Cuckoo Filter}, which optimizes the entire insertion pipeline by steering both stages. At the placement stage, the filter compares the occupancy of both candidate buckets and inserts into the less loaded one, applying the power-of-two-choice principle to reduce how often eviction chains are triggered. At the eviction stage, the filter preferentially displaces the most recently inserted element, whose alternate bucket carries latent randomness that shortens the resulting chain. Because these two guided decisions target orthogonal bottlenecks, eviction frequency and eviction chain length, their benefits compose multiplicatively. Experiments on cuckoo filters with $2^{22}$ slots confirm that the fully guided insertion reduces per-insertion kicks by up to $3.1\times$ at 96\% load and cumulative total kicks by 63\% at the practical capacity ceiling of 95\% load, with negligible computational overhead.

item.title: SEOYUN: Refusal-Inducing Exam Documents for AI-Glasses Pipelines
item.description: Camera-equipped glasses can convert an examination page into a query to a vision-language model (VLM). Device detection addresses possession; a complementary question is whether an examination document can reduce the usefulness of an unauthorized capture. We present SEOYUN, an application-specific framework for refusal-inducing exam documents, with optical and encoder-level interventions as extensions. We use reverse jailbreaking to describe the direction of the objective: inducing abstention rather than bypassing refusal. Refusal induction and defensive visual prompt injection already have precedents; our contribution is a threat model, analytical limits, and an evaluation protocol for examination use. We distinguish refusal from correct-answer leakage, show why removing an added dummy option is not itself a reduction in the original answer space, and derive a sampling comparison under explicitly stated camera assumptions. The protocol separates digital, simulated, and physical inputs and requires held-out evaluation after subject-specific selection. A local CSAT candidate corpus and rendering harness have been prepared, but this version reports no model-performance measurements, physical validation, or human-subject results. Accordingly, SEOYUN is a research framework, not a validated defense or a basis for allegations against individuals.

item.title: Blind tests of a simple-body model of submarine target strength on open benchmarks
item.description: Finite-element and boundary-element models of a submarine's sonar echo need a mesh and a solver, and their cost grows quickly with frequency. SSR-Sim takes an analytical route. The hull is cut into a few simple bodies, the echo of each is a closed-form result of geometrical acoustics or of the Kirchhoff approximation, the surface enters through a plane-wave reflection coefficient, and the echoes add in energy. This paper describes the method, including the reduction of a hull and its sail to simple bodies, and tests it on three open cases. (1) The reflection coefficient of a 50 mm rubber tile on steel plating, computed with finite elements by Yang et al., is reproduced to 0.02 rms or better at incidence angles from 0° to 75° once the layer is allowed to refract. (2) For the rigid full-scale BeTSSi submarine at 1 kHz, a prediction fixed before the reference was opened agrees with the boundary-element results of Venås and Kvamsdal to within 0.7 dB in every aspect sector from the bow to 150°; in the stern sector it is 5 dB high. (3) For a 1:15 BeTSSi model with 10 mm tiles measured in a lake, a second blind prediction is within -3.1, +1.4 and -0.5 dB of the measured level over aspects 0-120° at 5, 15 and 20 kHz, against -3.1, +3.1 and +3.5 dB for the Kirchhoff-finite-element computation published with the measurement. At 10 kHz, on a resonance of the tile, the prediction is 6.9 dB low, and in the bow sector it is 7 dB or more low at every frequency. The tests cover the specular component and the coating model only. The failures show what such a model lacks: edge diffraction and the returns that set the off-beam floor of a real model.

item.title: Closing Gaps in Temporal Fair Division for Chores
item.description: We study the fair division of indivisible chores that must be assigned in a prescribed order. The complete instance is known in advance, but assignments cannot be changed. Temporal envy-freeness up to one chore (TEF1) requires envy-freeness up to one chore after every arrival. For goods, TEF1 allocations need not exist, and deciding whether one exists is NP-hard. For chores, Elkind et al. (AAMAS 2025) showed that TEF1 allocations exist for two agents, but left open whether they always exist, conjecturing that they do not, and whether deciding their existence is hard. We resolve both questions, confirming the conjecture in a strong form: for every $n\ge3$ and every finite factor, some $n$-agent instance admits no allocation satisfying TEF1 even up to that factor. This holds even when all agents have the same multiset of individual chore costs, with nine chores sufficing for three agents. Deciding TEF1 existence is NP-complete for every fixed $n\ge3$, even when all costs lie within a factor $1+2^{-m}$ of one another, where $m$ is the number of chores. Instances without TEF1 allocations exist arbitrarily close to the uniform cost matrix with $O(n\log n)$ chores, and just nineteen for three agents. We then relate fairness to social cost. Even when a TEF1 allocation is supplied, minimizing social cost subject to TEF1 admits no polynomial-time approximation within any factor polynomial in the number of chores unless P$=$NP, already for three agents with strictly positive normalized costs. In contrast, for every fixed number of agents, we give an FPTAS for the optimal temporal EF1 factor, the smallest factor up to which TEF1 can be satisfied, whose output has social cost no larger than that of the cheapest allocation attaining this factor. Thus a slight relaxation of fairness permits a social-cost guarantee that, unless P$=$NP, no polynomial-time algorithm can provide under exact TEF1.

item.title: Sorting by block-reversals: closing the gap
item.description: In block-reversal sorting an elementary operation is to reverse the order of a contiguous block in a sequence, at cost proportional to the length of the block. In SODA 2004, Bender, Ge, He, Hu, Pinter, Skiena, and Swidan showed that every sequence of length $n$ can be sorted at cost $O(n\log^2{n})$ and some sequences can only be sorted at cost $Ω(n\log{n})$. In block-partition sorting, an elementary operation is to partition the sequence into contiguous blocks, and simultaneously reverse all blocks. The model was introduced in SODA 2024 by Jelínek, Opler, and Pekárek, who showed that every sequence can be sorted in $O(\log^2{n})$ steps and some sequences require $Ω(\log{n})$ steps. We close both gaps, showing that the upper bounds are tight, and the $\log^2{n}$ factors are unavoidable.

item.title: Self-Replicating Language Models
item.description: Whether large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are a form of life is a scientifically interesting question. Under the Darwinian definition of life, it is also a practical one, because a system capable of Darwinian Evolution can adapt. We therefore test several modes in which a language model can reproduce itself: by emitting a genome that trains its offspring, by copying and mutating its own weights, and by teaching a child from its own samples. In principle, small language models can replicate and evolve: selection improves them, and they adapt to narrow niches. Selection also lowers mutation rates, and a language model, unlike any organism, can lower its own to zero, which may limit its evolution. Flagship LLMs can write such replicators, but for a large LLM to replicate by teaching its offspring remains, for now, technically and economically infeasible.

item.title: Beyond Alignment: Whitening Geometry, Profile Synthesis, and Heterogeneous Ensembles for Cross-Environment WiFi Action Recognition
item.description: Cross-environment deployment is the central obstacle to practical WiFi sensing: a pipeline reaching 0.89+ top-1 in its training environments collapses to 0.408 under Leave-One-Domain-Out (LODO) evaluation with only K-shot labels. A ceiling analysis shows the collapse is not an alignment problem: the action signal is strong across seen environments (about 0.89 K10), environment identity is decodable from the encoder (0.965), and the failure concentrates in the encoder's extrapolation to the novel environment. A pre-registered falsification chain confirms that "align the domains" methods--training-time alignment, readout-level prototype alignment, adversarial confusion, and covariance/subspace alignment (CORAL -3.8pp, subspace -8.3pp)--degrade performance, and that source-domain statistics anti-correlate with cross-environment contribution. The effective levers lie elsewhere; we combine them into Dec-H: (i) closed-form source within-class whitening, provably re-geometrizing the readout's L2 regularization (+8.6pp, zero cost); (ii) profile-mixing augmentation (+1.0pp); (iii) few-shot adaptation with alternating whitening refit (+1.5pp; fixed preconditioners are 20/20 negative); (iv) heterogeneous decision ensembles (+1.7pp); homogeneous scaling and source-weighted stacking are saturated or harmful. Dec-H reaches 0.560 K10 (0.812 K40), +15.2pp over the baseline, consistent across all four environments and seeds; all thirteen configurations were pre-registered with frozen criteria.

item.title: Anchor and Check: Deterministic Cross-Prompt, Cross-Model Reconciliation for Auditable LLM Decisions
item.description: Pipelines that let a large language model (LLM) make discrete decisions need to know which decisions they may act on unattended, and a record that explains each one. We study a small, fully specified reconciliation contract: commit the target model's greedy answer (the anchor), draw one or two greedy checks that reach the answer by a different route (an alternate prompt, or a model from another family), and let a pure function return one of five outcomes, of which only Agree is acted on. On 48,000 model-item evaluations over 6,000 questions, with every method given access to verbalized confidence as a tie-breaker, the main finding concerns where calls come from: pooling another family's samples raises semantic entropy's AUROC by 1.7 to 4.0 points at every budget, and a same-model temperature check is the weakest design. As complete pipelines, the point estimates of the three-call contract and pooled semantic entropy over 3 or 5 samples differ by less than one point, with intervals containing zero. As detectors of the anchor's errors, the contract is ahead of pooled entropy with 3 and 5 samples under both tie-breaker conventions; with 10 samples the point estimates differ by less than one point and the sign depends on the convention. Under the strict Agree gate it automates 70% of items and still acts on 16% of errors. What the contract adds is a fixed committed answer, an explicit outcome and a decision replayable from its record; generation itself was not reproducible on the hosted API.

item.title: Fast and Accurate Body Estimation in Pixels, World Space and Scenes
item.description: We present FAB (Fast and Accurate Body estimation), a human body estimator that jointly improves inference efficiency and body-recovery fidelity. Rather than predicting only parametric mesh-model parameters, FAB directly predicts human skeleton joints and dense surface points. In images, it predicts dense 2D and 3D body points alongside a parametric Momentum Human Rig (MHR) head, then fits SMPL in one learned pass followed by two Gauss-Newton steps. Its ViT-L student, FAB-L, distilled from a fine-tuned SAM 3D Body, runs in real time for one person on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, from detection to a fitted body, at 4.6x the speed of SAM 3D Body's eager-PyTorch body-only path, while improving accuracy on most camera-space benchmarks. The same network predicts heel, toe, hand, and knee contacts, which connect the body to the scene. FAB also estimates world-space motion, fuses static-scene depth around the visible person, and aligns body and scene using predicted contacts. For human-to-humanoid real-to-sim transfer, an in-model G1 head and FAB-Retarget, a motion-level retargeter that reads dense points or the fitted mesh, map motion to a Unitree G1. FAB-Retarget produces references that follow the person more closely than specialized retargeters including SOMA, GMR, UMR, and OmniRetarget, and substantially more closely than Fast SAM 3D Body retargeted with our sequence IK. Project page: https://www.jinkuncao.com/FAB.

item.title: Computational trust as intuitionistic knowledge
item.description: In this paper, we will argue that the notion of computational trust can be understood as a form of fallible intuitionistic knowledge grounded in verification. This approach naturally captures a key aspect of trust: it involves vulnerability. Specifically, it validates the principle that verification leads to trust but does not validate the opposite principle that trust leads to verification. Thus, we can trust on good grounds that some program will perform according to its specification but the program might still fail. We present a simple logic for capturing this notion of computational trust based on constructive modal propositional logic extended with a trust modality, which will be specified in an inferential fashion and by utilizing the proofs-as-programs correspondence.

item.title: How Reliable Are Explanations of Language Models That Detect Insider Threats?
item.description: Organizations monitor their workers' activity for insider threats, in which workers misuse their legitimate access, by copying confidential files before leaving. Detectors score how unusual each day of activity is, flagging the most unusual for an analyst to review. Prominent current approaches use opaque neural networks, so explanations of a flag point to internal features: patterns of neuron activity most active on days of misuse. We audit such explanations for language-model detectors trained on CERT's simulated workplace logs. To test an explanation, we see what happens to the detector's score when we remove its features inside the model. We compare this to a control: a change that is as similar as possible to the removal, but without actually removing the features. Because defining "similar" requires choosing a metric, our central contribution is the tipping radius: a first-order prediction of how far that metric must move before the difference between removal and control disappears, a measure of how fragile the result is to that choice. In 33 of 34 runs of seven language models, the tipping radius is at most 18% of the distance between two standard choices of metric. Moving that far removes at least 58% of the difference or reverses it, while random moves of the same size leave it largely intact. The result replicates in thirteen of fourteen pre-declared primary runs on openly released models, though on our trained detectors the difference is often too small to measure. We also find that a flag's score partly reflects who the worker is, not what they did, and that the features named depend on whom they are compared against. Audits should therefore fix the control's metric in advance, report its tipping radius, and disclose that comparison.

item.title: Disentangling Monitor Hardware Artifacts and Smoothing Lag for Shift-Robust Intraoperative EEG and Hemodynamic Risk Calibration
item.description: Commercial intraoperative electroencephalography (EEG) and blood pressure monitors introduce cyclic impedance pulses, smoothing delays, direct-current (DC) drift, and cuff holds that confound risk forecasting and uncertainty calibration. We developed a causal signal-conditioning and shift-robust conformal calibration framework across 5,439 public anesthesia procedures. Streaming filters blank 10.13-min 64-Hz impedance checks, apply unclipped post-notch conditioning, separate 63-s suppression-ratio lag, and distinguish three-channel cuff inflations from dropouts across propofol-remifentanil total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA; N = 3,214), volatile anesthesia (N = 2,046), European endoscopy sedation (N = 171), and DC-coupled surgery (N = 8). De-impedanced cortical tree ensembles were compared against deep sequence models, paired with patient-cluster Subgroup-Covariate-Weighted Conformal Risk Control (CRC) and lag-buffered online Conformal Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) tracking. Pre-filter blanking removed 97.90% and 97.60% of false flatline conflicts while preserving 99.23% and 98.96% of deep suppression. On unseen TIVA surgeries (N = 525), cortical features achieved area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) 0.3135 (1.94% prevalence) and 0.1627 (0.82% lag-free prevalence), with no detectable difference from deep encoders (p >= 0.36) and no cortical gain for hypotension (0.3432 vs. 0.3437, p = 0.784). Zero-retraining volatile transfer (N = 1,048) showed no detectable difference from an end-tidal gas oracle on lag-free suppression (0.0820 vs. 0.0736, p = 0.472). Subgroup-Covariate-Weighted CRC bounded all 70 TIVA shift cells at <= 4.38% (alpha = 5.0%) in 66.32 ms per 30-s epoch. Causal artifact disentangling and shift-aware conformal calibration support reliable real-time intraoperative risk bounds within explicit physiological observability limits.

item.title: Uniqueness, Proximity, and Scaling in Atomic Splittable Polymatroid Congestion Games
item.description: We give a polynomial-time algorithm for exact equilibrium computation in atomic splittable polymatroid congestion games with integral ranks and rational player-specific affine latencies with positive slopes. The algorithm first computes equilibria of associated integer-splittable games, in which demands are allocated in multiples of a common packet size. For arbitrary polymatroid bases, no polynomial-time algorithm for these discrete equilibria was previously known. We provide such an algorithm and use progressively finer packets to recover the continuous equilibrium exactly. Our proof uses the multiple-exchange theorem of Oki and Schwarcz (2025) to obtain two exchange matchings that yield equilibrium proximity under changes of packet sizes and ranks, independently of cost coefficients. We then bound the matching deficiency caused by rank changes and construct compatible submodular rank roundings. Together these give a polynomial-time packet-halving algorithm using polynomially many submodular-function minimizations and exact rational arithmetic. The analysis rests on a uniqueness theorem of independent interest: for arbitrary real polymatroid ranks and continuously differentiable, strictly increasing, convex latencies, we prove uniqueness of equilibria, resolving a previously open problem.

item.title: Verification Behavior Across Five Qwen2.5-Instruct Checkpoints
item.description: We evaluate five Qwen2.5-Instruct checkpoints (0.5B to 32B) under four prompting conditions using three fixed tasks per information condition and five generations per task. Two AI raters scored 600 trajectories. Under the coordinated instruction, both raters recorded strict declarations of insufficiency in 11/15 cases at 7B, 0/15 at 14B, and 5/15 at 32B. The runner sent a standard follow-up when a request detector fired. The three checkpoints received at least one follow-up in 15, 12, and 15 cases, respectively. On information-sufficient tasks at 3B through 32B, scored format markers appeared in 60/60 protocol trajectories and 0/60 baseline trajectories. After adjudication, 1/60 in each condition met the diagnostic-execution criterion (H3). Across all checkpoints and prompts, 7/300 information-sufficient trajectories met H3 after adjudication, all on the same task. The prespecified upward transition did not occur in this run. The results separate visible structure, diagnostic execution, and persistence after a request for evidence.

item.title: Embodied Human-Data Interaction
item.description: We propose the concept of human-data interaction (HDI) as the human manipulation, analysis, and sensemaking of large, unstructured, and complex datasets. We then proceed to suggest an embodied approach to HDI to build physical reasoning environments for these difficult and polymorphic tasks. We illustrate our approach with two examples: tangible lenses for visual exploration, and an educational computer game with tangible bricks.

item.title: Beyond geometric lattices: pseudo-atoms and redundant join representations in the face lattice of the permutohedron
item.description: We study the lattice obtained from the poset of ordered set partitions (the Fubini poset), ordered by merging adjacent blocks, by adjoining a bottom element of rank -1. It is the face lattice of the permutohedron. We look at it from the point of view of geometric lattices: it is graded, atomic and coatomic in the strong sense that every element is a meet of coatoms, but it is not semimodular. Its atoms are the $n!$ permutations, and its elements of rank one, which we call pseudo-atoms, are the edges of the permutohedron. Describing ordered set partitions by chains of subsets, the cuts, we show that the rank is modular whenever the meet is above $\bot$, while the join of two distant atoms can have large rank, so that the rank of the join is a metric on permutations. An element has a unique representation as a join of atoms only up to rank one; above it, irredundant representations have sizes ranging from two to the rank, and the redundancy of an element is its number of atoms minus two. The Möbius function is that of an Eulerian lattice, the Whitney numbers are the face numbers of the permutohedron, and the characteristic polynomial has the alternating coefficients of the geometric case, but only $\bot$ and $\top$ are left-modular, so the lattice is not supersolvable. We show that it is CL-shellable, we exhibit EL-labelings for $n\le5$, and we compare the independent sets of Raz arXiv:2307.05005 (v3, Jan. 2026) with irredundant families and with the matroid of the vertices of the permutohedron. Replacing ordered set partitions by partial flags of subspaces of $\mathbb F_q^n$ gives a $q$-analogue, whose Möbius function is $(-1)^{\mathrm{rk}+1}q^κ$, with $κ$ the number of pairs of elements in a common block at $q=1$, and whose characteristic polynomial and Betti numbers are polynomials in $q$.

item.title: On the Hamel Coefficients and the Boltzmann-Hamel Equations for the Rigid Body
item.description: The Boltzmann-Hamel (BH) equations are central in the dynamics and control of nonholonomic systems described in terms of quasi-velocities. The rigid body is a classical example of such systems, and it is well-known that the BH-equations are the Newton-Euler (NE) equations when described in terms of rigid body twists as quasi-velocities. It is further known that the NE-equations are the Euler-Poincare, respectively, the reduced Euler-Lagrange equations on SE(3) when using body-fixed or spatial representation of rigid body twists. The connection between these equations are the Hamel coefficients, which are immediately identified as the structure constants of SE(3). However, an explicit coordinate-free derivation has not been presented in the literature. In this paper the Hamel coefficients for the rigid body are derived in a coordinate-free way without resorting to local coordinates describing the rigid body motion. The three most relevant choices of quasi-velocities (body-fixed, spatial, and hybrid representation of rigid body twists) are considered. The corresponding BH-equations are derived explicitly for the rotating and free floating body. Further, the Hamel equations for nonholonomically constrained rigid bodies are discussed, and demonstrated for the inhomogenous ball rolling on a plane.

item.title: Multiple Criteria Decision Making Under XORness
item.description: How should we make decisions under XORness? XORness is a class of uncertainty arising from indeterminacy, exclusivity, and hesitancy. We develop a multiple criteria decision making framework that preserves XORness throughout the decision process. We define XOR numbers and prove their fundamental arithmetic and algebraic properties. Building on these results, we extend the deterministic decision matrix to an XOR decision matrix and introduce a compatible normalization procedure. Further, we propose an additive XOR aggregation operator, which preserves indeterminacy, exclusivity, and hesitancy inherent in evaluations. In addition, we introduce an axiomatic XORness measure that quantifies the degree of uncertainty associated with global performance scores and develop a performance--XORness index to rank alternatives. We prove that this index induces a total preorder over the set of alternatives and identify the conditions for preserving dominance. The applicability of the developed framework is demonstrated through the risk assessment of cyberthreat scenarios in energy systems, and recommendations are derived using the XOR--weighted sum method.

item.title: Generative News Recommendation Reproduces Popularity: A Memorization-Based Analysis
item.description: Text-based generative recommenders can go beyond ranking existing items by directly generating item titles or other textual representations. In the news domain, this raises a societal concern that models may repeatedly surface already popular articles and thereby narrow the diversity of information to which users are exposed. We investigate training-data memorization as one mechanism behind this concentration. Using approximately 20 million browsing sessions from a Japanese news service, we continually trained an instruction-tuned Llama 3 8B model to generate the next article title in a session. The generated-title distribution was more concentrated and less diverse than the distribution of titles observed in the browsing logs. Frequently repeated target titles exhibited greater verbatim and approximate memorization, and more strongly memorized titles were generated in response to a wider range of prompts. These findings support a pathway in which popularity in behavioral logs becomes repeated training text, is preferentially memorized, and is subsequently reproduced by a generative recommender. An exploratory target-level deduplication condition reduced both memorization and output concentration, while substantially reducing the training-set size and recommendation accuracy. Our results suggest that popularity bias in generative recommendation may arise not only from user preferences or ranking objectives, but also from the model's tendency to reproduce frequently encountered strings, with important implications for information diversity on news platforms.

item.title: AI-Driven Transformation of Digital Platform Work: A Task-Based Model for Measuring Labour Disruption and Vulnerability, with Early Evidence from Online Freelancing in Kenya
item.description: Assessments of AI's impact on labour often rely on conventional occupational categories or broad market indicators. This dominant trend, however, obscures how tasks within the same occupation vary in practice across work arrangements. This limitation is particularly important in online freelancing, where workers are typically remote and devote substantial time performing unpaid tasks. This article introduces a task-based framework that distinguishes AI-driven disruption, defined as the extent of change in how work is performed, from livelihood vulnerability associated with that change. The framework is subsequently applied to assess the potential for automation, substitution, and enhancement across four categories of platform work: writing, virtual assistance, transcription, and web and software development. The model estimates high disruption across all four categories, while livelihood vulnerability scores are lower and vary by occupation. Potential efficiency gains on unpaid tasks partly offset potential wage impact associated with paid work in the model. The article compares these estimates with evidence from a survey of 52 online freelancers and 20 follow-up interviews in Nairobi, Kenya. Workers report changes in how they perform tasks and intensifying competition, while their accounts show how adapting their skills and using AI strategically shape their concerns about job loss. The findings show how task-based modelling can provide a baseline for assessing AI-driven changes in platform work and how workers' experiences differ from projections and help explain how these changes may threaten their livelihoods.

item.title: AZOWL AgentOps: Task-Scoped Governance for Deployed Agent Applications
item.description: AZOWL AgentOps provides shared governance for deploying agents and delegating work to them. Human and agent senders can exchange messages or explicitly delegate a business task. Accepted work has a stable identifier that links the sender's authority, the assigned runner, any required approval, and result evidence. The default enrolled customer PC profile is read-only. We compare AZOWL components with a configured LangGraph application in 28 synthetic runs across four paired pilots. Original AZOWL services checked work admission, recipient routing, and workflow prerequisites in isolated tests. The configured LangGraph application supplied business task and dispatch records in application code. Both configurations recorded zero business tasks in dialogue, rejected unauthorized agent handoffs, and issued zero writes when an approved delivery address changed. AZOWL's scope gate, exercised as a component, requested approval again on the same task. A product probe reused one registered provider across two workflows and checked prerequisite enforcement for ticket-task submission. The paired protected writes, including ticket creation, used mock providers. Of two deployed PC inventory reads with verified receipts, we traced the 0.6.57 run from submission through runner pickup and tool execution to the receipt, with matching local and central artifact hashes. A separate deployed GRC audit followed an operator-driven ticket lifecycle on sample records.

item.title: Passing NPCR Without Diffusion: Exact Signatures, a Detection Benchmark and an Audit of Published Image Ciphers
item.description: NPCR, the share of ciphertext bytes changed by a one-pixel plaintext change, is reported for nearly every image cipher as evidence of diffusion, with 99.61% the target. Several mechanisms produce values near it, and the mean does not say which. We separate three regimes: no propagation, one round of forward and backward chaining linear over addition or XOR, and independent ciphertexts. For the second an exact count applies. After a least-significant-bit change its mean asymptotically matches the independent-ciphertext reference, while its spread without cancellation is about five to twenty times larger. In simulation, the one-sided NPCR test of Wu, Noonan and Agaian flags one-round additive, mixed and S-box chaining in 2-4% of papers; read in both directions, the same five values flag at least 99.9%. Two-sided testing does the detecting; the spread and the other signatures help diagnose the structure. We then audit twenty-one published schemes. The count matches a reimplementation of one published diffusion layer on every trial and accounts for its reported table, the signatures show two schemes whose printed specifications cannot produce their reported values, and find that three of our own report plain-versus-cipher values and fall to two chosen images; ten more change their encryption material with the plaintext or per encryption, so their NPCR mostly reflects that change. A released checker applies the signatures to published tables, showing what a table measures within stated assumptions; it does not certify security.

item.title: Dynamics of Protected State Evolution
item.description: States with identical protected observations can admit different future interventions. Each transition specifies its successor, response increment, required initial reserve and net consumption. Composing these records in execution order distinguishes protocols with equal net consumption and different initial reserve requirements. At a fixed state, a weighted Gram operator determines the linear response ellipsoid and a quotient identifies directions attainable only through cooperation between blocks. Nonlinear systems with identical complete affine data can have incomparable finite-budget response sets. In regular charts, the first correction to quadratic minimum cost is a covariant cubic form involving the third derivative of cost and the Hessians of protection and response. At singular gates, sequential feasibility depends on the peak reserve along the path. A history-weighted operator detects responses outside the old channel's range closure. Controlled congruence characterizes exact reductions of deterministic labelled dynamics, and a two-cut value identity separates the effect of paid verification from that of subsequent action selection. On Qwen2.5-7B Base, two projected policies preserved 2,048 reference top tokens under a per-position KL ceiling of $2\times10^{-5}$. Over 200 arrivals they recovered 391 of 396 initial rejections. Each yielded over 1,200 times the held-out cross-entropy reduction of historical-channel-only AdamW. Under an expanded 2,560-position contract, fixed continuation and neutral renewal began on the same protected logit fiber in distinct structural strata. Both admitted all 200 subsequent writes. Fixed continuation yielded 1.74 times the held-out loss reduction per unit squared write cost. Renewal had a smaller KL excess on the first candidate tested at every arrival and used fewer full verification scans.

item.title: DRVEXO-4B-Unified: Design and Evaluation of a Modular Speech-Vision System
item.description: We present DRVEXO-4B-Unified, a modular multimodal assistant built around a 4B language backbone. A self-contained checkpoint combines text, image, and speech inputs with reference-conditioned speech output and structured interaction. A temporal residual connector adapts acoustic sequences to the language interface; explicit text boundaries support incremental speech synthesis; and three task-conditioned scoring heads rank supplied action candidates alongside generative tool calls. These interfaces connect conversation to application-defined choices while leaving action authorization to the application. The system obtains 74.22% on all 900 MMMU validation questions, exceeding the published validation scores of Gemma 3 4B IT and InternVL3.5-4B without test-time scaling. Strict prompt-level IFEval accuracy is 82.26% and MATH-500 accuracy is 89.40%, above the original Qwen3-4B non-thinking report's 81.2% and 84.8%, respectively. On NVIDIA GB10, the model achieves a speech-synthesis first-chunk latency of 390 ms. For concurrent text generation, a growth-aware admission policy completes a 128-answer batch at 594.41 output tokens/s, including filling and draining, without preemptions. We plan to release the model weights and accompanying code under Apache License 2.0, retaining applicable third-party terms.

item.title: When and why can integral constraints improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks?
item.description: Adding constraints obtained by integrating governing equations to the loss has been reported to improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in several applications, but mathematical understanding of these benefits remains limited. For several partial differential equations (PDEs), we derive stability estimates for losses with and without integral constraints. The comparison reveals that in certain parameter regimes, the standard loss has very weak control over specific error components, and that the integral constraints restore uniform control of these components. This explains when and why the constraints improve accuracy. Finally, numerical experiments support this interpretation. In parameter regimes where the standard loss is predicted to have weak control over those components, the two losses indeed show clear differences in accuracy. Conversely, in regimes where the standard loss retains sufficient control, both losses yield similar accuracy.

item.title: LingSante MedGuard Technical Report
item.description: As medical AI is increasingly used for patient consultation and clinical decision support, identifying harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic responses is essential for responsible deployment. Assessing these risks requires checking clinical claims against relevant evidence, verifying calculations, and applying medical requirements under their intended conditions. We introduce LingSante MedGuard, a capability-enhanced guardrail that integrates supervision from a medical guardrail teacher model and six specialized medical capability experts into a unified model. The guardrail teacher supervises risk decisions and explanations across medical safety, compliance, and ethics, while the capability experts support medical rule understanding, numerical reasoning, multimodal hallucination detection, agentic safety verification, risk localization, and multimodal entity understanding. We consolidate these sources of supervision through offline supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated demonstrations, followed by multi-teacher on-policy distillation using feedback on student-generated responses. We further introduce LingSante MedGuardBench, a benchmark comprising 11 risk-detection subsets spanning medical safety, compliance, and ethics. At 4B, 9B, and 27B scales, LingSante MedGuard achieves mean benchmark F1 scores of 82.3%, 82.4%, and 87.4%, respectively. The 4B model also achieves 73.9% mean accuracy across MedHallu and MedHALT-NOTA under retrieval-enabled evaluation. Additional evaluations of the verification components show improvements in evidence-supported consistency, source traceability, and rule-guided rationale quality across model scales. These results support the integration of specialized medical capabilities into a unified guardrail for medical risk assessment and evidence-based medical safety verification.

item.title: Persona Lenses: What Makes a Vision-Language Model See Through Its Persona's Eyes?
item.description: Vision-language models have been used to simulate where a user looks on a web page. However, a persona in the prompt reaches the simulated gaze only partly. We measure this reach as the difference in one model's gaze between two MatrAIx personas that differ in a single attribute. We introduce persona lenses, which place the persona between the model and the page: a text lens (a two-step prompt in which the model first writes what the persona would look at), a pixel lens (marks on the region matching the persona's interests) and a weight lens (a dwell reward gated to keep the scanpath natural). Using Qwen3-VL (4B and 32B) and Qwen3.5-9B on generated and live pages, we compare the lenses with one another and with scale, the 32B model with no lens. It has been confirmed that the text lens separates the personas strongly but is not robust to profile changes that should not move gaze. The pixel lens separates the personas less but is unaffected by attributes unrelated to gaze. At 4B and 9B, the weight lens separates the personas on interests held out from training, with no extra step on a new page. The 32B model separates the personas with the base prompt alone. Therefore, the choice of a lens depends on cost and model size.

item.title: Coordinated Use of Large Language Models in Academic Research
item.description: This study proposes a methodological framework for the coordinated use of multiple large language models in academic research. Its central argument is that involving more models does not in itself guarantee more reliable results; what matters is how cognitive and verification operations are organised. The framework is based on seven principles (procedural independence, functional allocation, the diagnostic value of divergence, the diagnostic value of convergence, external verification, proportionality of checking, and human epistemic responsibility) and sets out a non-linear multi-LLM protocol in which independently obtained results are compared, critically examined and, where necessary, verified against external sources. The approach is illustrated through real-world cases drawn from research practice. The study concludes that moving from a single language model to a coordinated multi-LLM process represents a change in the organisation of research, in which the researcher makes the final decisions and bears scholarly responsibility.

item.title: Convex splitting by binary quantum hypothesis testing
item.description: How many independent quantum systems does it take to hide one system that is correlated with a reference? An observer can measure all the systems together with the reference to detect the correlation. We turn any such measurement into binary tests on a single system and the reference. For each test we bound the probability of declaring a signal when an independent pair was prepared. Averaging the largest signal acceptance probabilities allowed by these bounds controls the normalized trace distance in the convex-split lemma. A second bound gives a sufficient number of systems by minimizing the hypothesis-testing relative entropy over the state of the reference. Both bounds hold for density operators on separable Hilbert spaces. Comparing two distributions for the location of the hidden system gives one-shot bounds for private communication and one-way secret key distillation, including the public information available to an eavesdropper. For a fixed finite-alphabet model with separable quantum outputs and positive information advantage and variances, we recover the known Gaussian corrections to the attainable number of private or key bits from $n$ independent repetitions and bound the remaining loss by $\log_2 n+O(1)$ at fixed errors. The position-based key distillation protocol attains this bound with $O(n)$ public bits.

item.title: Planning Width Is Hard to Approximate Even Given the Unique Optimal Plan
item.description: For each fixed $k$, iterative-width search finds optimal plans in polynomial time on tasks of bounded tuple-chain width, but the approximability of planning width has remained open even when an optimal plan is supplied. When all optimal plans visit the same state sequence, we characterize set and chain width as hitting numbers of competing states. We construct positive-precondition STRIPS tasks with a supplied unique optimal plan, a single reachable goal state, binary branching, and constant-size actions. Every reachable state lies on a goal-reaching execution at most one action longer than optimal, yet distinguishing width $1$ from $Θ(N)$, where $N$ is the number of atoms, is NP-hard for set, chain, and goal-admissible width. Unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, no polynomial-time algorithm achieves a one-sided approximation factor $o(N)$ or a symmetric factor $o(\sqrt{N})$, and simple estimates attain both orders. For positive-precondition tasks with a supplied unique optimal plan of length at least two, testing set or chain width against a threshold $k\geq 1$ is coNP-complete for each fixed $k$ and $Σ_2^{\mathrm{P}}$-complete when $k$ is part of the input. Both results also hold for goal-admissible width if only one goal state is reachable. On an explicit state graph, a greedy algorithm approximates set width within a logarithmic factor even when optimal plans branch. Thus, knowing an optimal plan does not eliminate the difficulty of certifying substantially smaller width.

item.title: Dimension-Free Buffer Bounds for Compressed-Momentum Error Feedback
item.description: Analyses of error feedback bound the memory buffer through a compressor contraction constant -- $r/p$ for the best rank-$r$ approximation of a $p$-dimensional spectrum -- which survives into the rate. We show it need not appear at all. When the compressed momentum is re-injected into the pre-compression accumulator, the previous compressed momentum $β_1 M_{t-1}$ is an admissible competitor in the projection, and the buffer obeys $\|E_t\|_F \le (1-β_1)\|G_t\|_F + γ\|E_{t-1}\|_F$, free of the dimensions $m,n$ and of the rank $r$. The argument uses only that the compressor is a metric projection onto a closed cone, so it covers top-$k$ selection as well as truncated SVD, holds for every selection from the projection set with no condition on singular-value crossings, and in its trajectory-tracking form assumes nothing about the gradients. In the two-stage template of the standard analyses it replaces a Stage-2 constant of order $p^2/r^2$ by one of order $1$, against $Θ(p/r)$ for the sharpest contraction-based bounds. Transferring the full rate costs a leakage term, which we bound by the step-weighted gradient mass $\sum_{u\le t}η_u\|G_u\|_F$ and show tight up to a factor $\sqrt{2}$; the price is an additive $O(\log^2 T)$ floor, not a slower rate. On BERT fine-tuning at rank ratio $32/768$ the feedback decay costs under $0.008$ validation $F_1$.

item.title: LoongForge-Embodied: A Unified Framework for Training Heterogeneous Embodied Models
item.description: Training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs) is computationally expensive, while their heterogeneous architectures and fragmented training stacks make system optimizations difficult to reuse across models. To address these challenges, we present LoongForge-Embodied, a native-PyTorch framework that unifies and accelerates the training of heterogeneous embodied models. At its core, LoongForge-Embodied introduces a common abstraction layer that decouples model-specific implementations from shared training infrastructure, enabling cross-model reuse without constraining individual architectures or execution requirements. Buildingon this unified infrastructure, the framework combines reusable acceleration mechanisms with model-specific and hardware-aware optimization strategies across computation, execution, memory, data I/O, and distributed communication, including FP8-based communication optimizations for DDP and FSDP. Beyond training acceleration, LoongForge-Embodied integrates a unified data infrastructure with a pipeline for synthesizing robot data from egocentric data, and an efficient evaluation framework that supports concurrency and optimized computation in simulator. Experiments across representative VLA and WAM models demonstrate 1.47x-4.38x end-to-end training throughput improvements over their corresponding open-source baselines, as well as 4.1x-23.2x faster evaluation under the same protocols.

item.title: Interference Bounds and Merge-Aware Training Dynamics for Composable Fine-Tuned Models
item.description: Combining fine-tuned models by composing their parameter updates has become a standard alternative to multi-task training. We formalize composability as a property of a collection of task vectors and prove that the excess loss of the merged model is controlled by an interference functional of the cross-task curvature overlap and the signed alignment of the updates. In the quadratic regime this functional equals the excess loss, giving a criterion that is necessary as well as sufficient and that measures the angle between task vectors in the curvature metric rather than the Euclidean one. Fine-tuning under a curvature-guided regularizer -- constructed from curvature statistics of the kind memory-efficient optimizers maintain -- keeps displacement in the base curvature metric below a ceiling set by the penalty coefficient at every iterate, at the standard $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ non-convex rate. Under a single Loewner comparison between the base statistic and the task curvatures, this control converts into a ceiling on the interference functional, inversely proportional to the penalty coefficient, so that the curvature term of the bound is controlled during training. A first-order term, present because regularized solutions are not stationary for the task loss, is not reduced in the same way. Experiments on an exact non-quadratic model confirm the budget and the ceiling, show the first-order term dominating for strong penalties, and find the curvature-guided penalty slightly better than an isotropic one. In a three-seed transformer study the functional is rank-correlated with merging degradation, but no more strongly than the Euclidean displacement norm.

item.title: Instance-Optimal Moment Estimation in the Add-Remove Model of Differential Privacy
item.description: In this paper, we study the problem of estimating empirical means, variances, and covariances under pure differential privacy in the add-remove model. While existing mechanisms achieve optimal worst-case error, they may not be optimal for individual datasets. To measure the performance of mechanisms on individual datasets, we introduce instance-dependent error metrics and prove sharp lower bounds on them. Then, we design mechanisms that achieve these lower bounds and demonstrate that they achieve asymptotically better utility compared to existing methods.

item.title: Falsifiable Compositional Reasoning in Time Series Forecasting
item.description: Time series foundation models as well as the language-guided analytical agents achieve strong accuracy on standard chronological benchmarks. However, models that rank highest on historical validation splits often degrade across non-stationary regime transitions. We hypothesise that this gap arises from using historical backtesting as an open-ended search and model-selection objective instead of using it to test pre-specified compositional assumptions. Real-world time series are generated by recurring latent primitives that co-move within finite historical windows. Under strong historical co-movement, chronological holdout error cannot separate predictors that learn invariant couplings among primitives from predictors that fit transient historical correlations. Searching over large pools of architectures, hyperparameters, or chain-of-thought rules further biases selection toward historical shortcuts. Through theoretical analysis and diagnostic experiments on a controlled multi-primitive benchmark and German day-ahead electricity prices, we show that expanding validation search fails to improve out-of-regime accuracy, and that decomposing primitives without an ex-ante falsification test still breaks down when residual correlations shift. Hence, we propose formulating time series forecasting and reasoning around falsifiable compositional hypotheses that combine neural primitive encoders, explicit coupling constraints, and training-calibrated falsification tests.

item.title: Drifting, Discriminating, and Directioning for Action Coordination in Higher-dimensional Action Space
item.description: This paper proposes a lightweight policy model to mitigate the difficulty of handling higher-dimensional action spaces in reinforcement learning (RL), alongside an algorithm to effectively train it. To address this, we focus on drifting models, which can implicitly represent complex distributions and infer actions in a single forward pass. However, while drifting models can be straightforwardly trained via backpropagation of the Q-gradient, this alone cannot be expected to appropriately capture the desired action coordination. Therefore, this paper constructs a three-step learning algorithm to encourage the action coordination. First, the source distribution of the drifting model is co-optimized as a diagonal policy model. This conditions the drifting model to attach the coordination, which cannot be expressed by a diagonal distribution, as residuals. Second, a discriminator model before and after drifting is introduced with adversarial training for a regularization term. This actively promotes the extraction of the coordination that fundamentally separates the two distributions. Third, best-of-N sampling is applied for action selection during rollouts in order to give directionality toward/beyond the regions where the coordination is insufficiently extracted/sufficiently discovered. The proposed method consistently improves the sample efficiency and the final control performance over the conventional diagonal distribution modeling across three locomotion tasks with high-dimensional action spaces. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that this improvement is achieved by reducing variance in certain action dimensions, effectively coupling them with other actions as action coordination.

item.title: Beyond Weight Updates: Evolving Agent Harnesses for Domain Specialization
item.description: Domain specialization of LLM agents is usually framed as a weight-update problem: collect trajectories, run reinforcement learning (RL) or supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and deploy a new checkpoint. We study a complementary axis: evolving the \textbf{agent harness}---the system prompt, tool schemas, skill library, and planning scaffolding---while keeping the policy frozen. We cast harness evolution as an RL-style outer loop and instantiate it with GEPA, a reflective evolutionary optimizer. The resulting harness adapters require no GPU training, are loadable per vertical domain, and compose with weight-based RL. Experiments with Codev, a Claude Code-style coding agent, on SWE-bench Verified, OfficeBench, and Terminal-Bench show a consistent pattern: weight updates give the strongest single-path gains, harness evolution recovers most of those gains at a small fraction of the compute, and combining both paths is best overall. We also analyze a failure mode of SFT-based specialization---shortened reasoning chains and increased truncation---and argue that harness adapters avoid it by construction. Our results position harness evolution as a practical, non-destructive complement to weight updates for vertical agents.

item.title: Fundamentals for Binary Classification Under Label Noise
item.description: This chapter surveys fundamental results for binary classification under label noise. Binary classification under label noise involves training models on datasets where class labels are partially incorrect, leading to degraded performance and misclassification. We distinguish poisoning attacks from noise processes and formalize random classification noise, Massart noise, and malicious classification noise within the probably approximately correct (PAC) framework. These models capture different adversarial strengths and data-generation realities. We then highlight some core ideas and representative results. In particular, we explain why random classification noise preserves the expected ordering of hypotheses and thus supports learning using the empirical risk minimization (ERM) principle, how sample complexity depends on the noise rate, and why learning algorithms often require an upper bound on the corruption level, as well as how such a bound may be estimated from data in the case of random classification noise. We also discuss computational aspects of ERM under noise and present a canonical negative result technique -- the method of induced distributions -- within the malicious noise model where the adversary has more power and may affect not only the label of an example but also the instance. We conclude with pointers to related work and a taxonomy that organizes classical label-noise models using the NCAR/NAR/NNAR lens.

item.title: Certified pandigital approximations of $π$, $γ$, $δ$ and $e$
item.description: In 2004 Erich Friedman asked for the best approximations of $π$, $e$, the Euler-Mascheroni constant $γ$ and Feigenbaum's constant $δ$ that use each of the digits $1,\dots,n$ exactly once, with addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, exponentiation, parentheses and the decimal point. We determine the optimal expressions for $π$, $γ$ and $δ$ for every $n \le 9$, with the digits in any order and in increasing order, and for $e$ when $n \le 6$. The optima are found by exhaustive search and certified by an independent algorithm that encloses every expression rigorously and decides each candidate with Arb and exact arithmetic; a second certified computation covers intermediate values of any size. Twenty-one entries improve the published records; for $π$ with the digits 1-9 the optimal error is $2.81\cdot 10^{-14}$. For $e$, whose records come from identities between power towers, we prove that Bamberger's formula is optimal within the natural family of such identities. All code and certificates are public.

item.title: Now You See Me Now You Don't: A Framework To Detect and Reduce Proxy Capacity
item.description: In regulated domains such as lending, the two most salient fairness concepts are disparate impact and disparate treatment: disparate impact is generally defined by differential rates of adverse outcomes between demographic groups, while disparate treatment is generally defined by the use of demographic information or proxies to issue decisions. There already exist established methods to quantitatively detect and mitigate disparate impact; however, there has been less research on doing the same for disparate treatment. From a practitioner's perspective, the manner in which a conditional independence test is formulated and operationalized to identify proxies is nuanced and underexplored. As Machine Learning (ML) systems increase in scope and application in regulated domains, practitioners need a defensible framework to identify proxies at scale. Current disparate treatment frameworks typically rely upon some combination of quantitative and qualitative review of models' inputs to identify proxies. Features that are identified as proxies are then typically removed from the model in practice, and predictive performance degrades in favor of fairness through unawareness. Here, we propose a two-part framework that reduces the disparate treatment risk of a feature and keeps the predictive performance that removal of the feature loses. First, we propose a quantitative test for proxy capacity that identifies whether some of a feature's values reveal membership in a particular demographic group. Second, we propose a pre-processing methodology that adjusts those proxy features to reduce their proxy capacity. We show empirically on synthetic and public datasets that this framework identifies features that proxy for demographic information and reduces their proxy capacity while the adjusted feature retains task-relevant signal (i.e. improves predictive performance versus removal).

item.title: When Should Deployed BCI Decoders Adapt? A Resource-Priced Ladder for Frozen EEG Trunks
item.description: When should a deployed MI decoder spend adaptation resources-not only how to adapt under shift? We study a thin control layer outside a frozen encoder: a resource ladder (factory -> Bayesian head -> affine map, with full fine-tune as an escape hatch) governed by regime-aware gating under a utility that prices accuracy, fit time, and label cost. The head is Bayesian in the conjugate sense: a Normal-Inverse-Wishart prior over the class conditional Gaussians in embedding space, updated in closed form (no gradients) as labelled trials arrive. Full estimators, constants, and the reanalysis code are in the companion paper and the ancillary bundle of this submission. Thesis: adaptation should be gated and capped, not always-on and not blindly fine-tuned. Evidence: (i) utility-max gating over-adapts on clean data that already carries session drift; a clean-referenced gate restores low false-entry rates (e.g. dropping the adaptation rate from 0.56 to 0.11 on field-like sessions, with the cascade staying on the factory decoder for ~87% of clean cells). (ii) Under severe synthetic stress, a lightweight LDA head matches or exceeds the frozen trunk's accuracy across five encoder architectures (n=155 subject x trunk cells, pooled across shared subjects), at ~23x lower fit time than full warm-start fine-tuning. Always-on baselines favor capping the default below full fine-tune. (iii) In two no-perturbation BNCI session checks the factory model transferred without intervention (no reliable head gain), so the control layer's value under natural drift is cost-efficiency and clean-safety rather than demonstrated accuracy gains. (iv) Adaptation severity does not follow a universal ordinal ladder across datasets, highlighting the need for dynamic gating over fixed adaptation policies.

item.title: Enhancing Understanding of Language Models with Varied Explanations
item.description: Language models are increasingly used to support human judgement in complex reasoning tasks, yet their predictions often remain difficult to interpret and validate. Explainability techniques provide insight into model decision-making, helping expose errors, failure modes, and potential bias so users can decide whether to rely on model outputs. Explanations are simplified approximations of a language model's internal workings. The goal is to obtain explanations that reflect the underlying computation as closely as possible (faithfulness), are understandable to users (plausibility), and help them achieve their intended goals (utility). Evaluation protocols are essential for assessing these dimensions. This thesis studies highlight explanations, natural language explanations, and chain-of-thought reasoning. These forms offer complementary perspectives on model behaviour and exhibit distinct strengths and limitations across tasks. Producing explanations that satisfy multiple quality dimensions remains challenging, as does evaluating them reliably across forms and settings. This thesis aims to improve people's understanding of models' decision-making processes in complex reasoning tasks. First, it proposes two evaluation frameworks for assessing highlight explanations across multiple properties and explanation types, together with a meta-evaluation framework for examining the reliability of existing faithfulness metrics for chain-of-thought explanations. Second, it proposes two techniques that generate natural language explanations designed to be faithful to the model's prediction process while remaining concise, coherent, and helpful for understanding model decisions. Finally, a study of human-AI interaction explores the roles of evidence and explanations in helping users validate model verdicts in a fact-checking setting.

item.title: Prescribed Bayesian Efficiency under Lifetime Adjustment Costs
item.description: A Bayesian learner may retain an issued action while updating its posterior, trading predictive loss against adjustment charges. We assume population curvature, boundary control, an order-$1/n$ lower bound on expected posterior uncertainty about the optimal action, and an observable unbiased gradient witness whose squared norms are uniformly integrable. Sample losses may be unbounded or nonconvex. Cumulative expected excess measures the loss increase relative to current predictive Bayes actions. For bounded nonnegative nondecreasing charges $c$ with $c(0)=0$ and nondecreasing profiles $G: \mathbb{N} \to [1,\infty)$ with $G(J)=o(J)$, we characterize joint attainability of cumulative expected excess $O(G(J))$ at horizons $T=2^J$ and finite expected lifetime charge. Here $J$ indexes logarithmic time. The criterion is finiteness of a prefix-constrained allocation of tracking-error allowances across action-distance scales, equivalently its decreasing-weight dual. Adaptive timing and private randomization do not enlarge the attainable region. For each feasible pair, a horizon-independent deterministic checkpoint policy attains the profile with lifetime-cost moments of every positive order. For excess $O((\log T)^r)$, $0<r<1$, every policy needs $Ω((\log T)^{2-r})$ revisions in expectation, and a charge-independent schedule achieves a matching pathwise upper bound for every feasible charge. We verify the assumptions for logistic decision models with nondegenerate covariates, finite second moments and a locally positive smooth prior density, including fixed-ridge models with unbounded parameter priors.

item.title: Subexponential Algorithms for Continuous Euclidean $k$-Means in Subpolylogarithmic Dimension
item.description: Given $n$ points in $\mathbb{Q}^d$ and an integer $k$, the continuous Euclidean $k$-means problem asks for $k$ centers in $\mathbb{R}^d$ that minimize the sum of squared distances from the input points to their nearest centers. In one dimension, the problem can be solved in polynomial time by dynamic programming. In higher dimensions, the algorithm of Inaba, Katoh, and Imai [SoCG 1994] runs in polynomial time when both $k$ and $d$ are fixed.
